title: Asymmetric Perturbation in Solving Bilinear Saddle-Point Optimization
claim: Symmetric perturbation moves away from the equilibrium as strength grows, but asymmetric perturbation keeps exact equilibrium below a threshold.
layout: 2 side-by-side line plots, shared x-axis, shaded invariance region with dashed threshold
description: Two side-by-side line plots share the same x-axis, the perturbation strength μ from 0 to 6, and the same y-axis label, NashConv for player x. Panel (a), Symmetric Perturbation, shows a single blue curve. It rises from near zero at small μ to a peak of about 0.23 near μ=3, dips to a kink at μ=5, then climbs again. The curve is never exactly zero. Panel (b), Asymmetric Perturbation, shows a flat blue line at exactly 0 for μ below about 2.5. A light red shaded region marked 'Equilibrium Invariance Regime' covers that range. A dashed red vertical line and a red dot mark the threshold. Past the threshold the curve rises smoothly. Italic captions (a) and (b) sit below the panels. The eye goes first to the red shaded region and the flat line in (b).
caption: The proximity of $x^{\mu}$ to $x^{\ast}$ under the symmetric perturbation and the asymmetric perturbation with varying $\mu$. The game matrix $A$ is given by $[[0, 1, -3], [-1, 0, 1], [3, -1, 0]]$. The proximity to the minimax strategy is measured by the value of $\max_{y\in \Y}(x^{\mu})^{\top}Ay - v^{\ast}$.
abstract: This paper proposes asymmetric perturbation, where only one player's payoff function is perturbed, for solving bilinear saddle-point optimization problems, commonly arising in minimax problems, game theory, and constrained optimization. Symmetric perturbation is known to require decreasing its strength to ensure convergence to a solution, i.e., an equilibrium in the original game, resulting in a slower rate. First, with asymmetric perturbation, we show that, for a sufficiently small perturbation strength, the equilibrium strategy of the asymmetrically perturbed game coincides with an equilibrium strategy of the original unperturbed game. Second, building on this coincidence, we construct a learning algorithm with a linear last-iterate convergence rate. Third, motivated by the fact that the coincidence relies on the perturbation strength being sufficiently small, we also provide a parameter-free variant, retaining the linear rate. Finally, we empirically demonstrate fast convergence toward equilibria in both normal-form and extensive-form games.
